Page 29 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program Vacuum Pump Types Vacuum is a significant consideration in EBW costs as it influences both the capital costs of the system through the pumps used, as well as the operational expenses of the system via time lost to pump down, i.e. cycle time. Minimizing the time needed to reach operating vacuum weld vacuum is a significant consideration, and estimates put the utiliziation time (welding time) of EBW at roughly 10% due to vacuum pump down times. EBW systems are composed of 2 vacuum systems for rough and high vacuum operation and includes the associated valves for switching between processes. A roughing pump skid such as a wet rotary vane pump or lubricant-free ‘dry’ scroll pump is used to achieve the pressure level required for the high vacuum pumps to operate. High vacuum pumps are generally one of three types: diffusion pumps, cryo pumps, and turbo pumps. Turbo pumps are generally used on small chambers as well as the gun itself, and quickly become uneconomical for large pumping speeds, which can often reach 10,000 L/s. Diffusion pumps are most commonly found on large volume chambers and require a high-quality silicon-based oil to avoid hydrocarbons contamination in the vacuum chamber and weld via backstreaming. Specialized diffusion pump oils such as Santovac 5 have been successfully used to weld SRF cavities with minimal contamination. Since cryopumps are dry, they provide cleanest vacuum (ie no backstraeming hydrocarbons) as well as very high pump speeds, but are generally costly and complex to maintain. Furthermore maintaining an ultrahigh vacuum during electron beam welding is not practical due to the challenges of performing a bakeout, as well as the intrinsic vaporization that occurs from the weld pool which limits vacuum levels to the 10-4 to 10-6 Torr range. Added vacuum components such as Roots blower or cold traps can also assist in reducing pumpdown time. The vacuum valves found on an EBW system can be expensive, especially the large diameter gate valves associated with diffusion or cryopumps. Most EBW systems include a gate valve between the chamber volume and the gun volume, allowing for rapid turn-around of parts by not venting the gun volume. The cost and maintenance of the valves, as well as the manually operated chamber doors, requires detailed maintenance protocols. Chamber Size EBW chamber size is one of the biggest considerations in terms of capital costs. Since these systems can occupy significant floor space, chamber size can also greatly influence the operational expense of the system as well.
